forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Leicester awarded £34.1m High Needs Stability Grant against a £37.9m schools funding deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Leicester City Council has been awarded a £34.1m High Needs Stability Grant, which its budget monitoring report says reduces the call on the council's own resources to £3.8m. The grant covers 90% of the £37.9m cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, at March 2026. The report says the Department for Education "were pleased" with the council's Local Area SEND Reform Plan, and notes that not all local authorities have secured this grant.

The same report, for the Overview Select Committee, forecasts an overspend of £34.9m for 2026/27 on the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. It also expects a £1.1m clawback of early years funding. Education, health and care plans, the legal documents setting out a child's support, numbered 4,080 at September 2026, up from 3,946 at March 2026.

The council has set aside reserves of £10m for dedicated schools grant deficits: £4.5m in 2025/26, £2.7m in 2026/27 and £2.8m in 2027/28. The report says the government has not yet confirmed conditions or amounts for further funding.

news_drafts.headline: Leicester's auditor closes its medium-term finance recommendation as council drops exceptional support plans
news_drafts.lead:
Leicester City Council no longer expects to need exceptional financial support in the foreseeable future, according to a draft annual audit report on its 2025/26 accounts. Exceptional financial support is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort. The report goes to the council's Governance and Audit Committee on 18 November 2026.

The report, dated 6 November 2026, says: "Due to the significantly improved financial position, the Council no longer envisages requiring exceptional financial support (EFS) in the foreseeable future."

The council's external auditor says that, because of the improved position, it does not consider there to be a significant weakness in the council's arrangements to address its medium-term financial challenge in 2025/26. It has also closed the key recommendation it made on the subject in the prior year. The draft report gives no figures for the improvement.

findings.paper_title: The Corporate Estate Annual Report FY25.26 FINAL
findings.headline: The £178.84m estate valuation is subject to the FY25/26 Annual Audit of Assets, to be completed in October 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the valuation will not be formally signed until it is reported to the Governance & Audit Committee in December 2026, and all figures and assumptions are subject to audit.
findings.matters: Any reader relying on the £178.84m valuation or the £24.4m uplift needs to know that the figures are unaudited until December 2026.
findings.figures: £178.84m valuation at 31 March 2026; audit completion October 2026; sign-off December 2026
findings.quote: The FY25/26 Annual Audit of Assets is in progress and will be completed in October 2026.

findings.paper_title: The Corporate Estate Annual Report FY25.26 FINAL
findings.headline: Government removed the 2027 EPC C milestone for commercial property, which the paper says allows the Council to defer planned capital works
findings.detail: The paper says the June 2026 revision to Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) removed the April 2027 EPC C mandate. Buildings over 1,000 square metres will now need EPC B by 2031, subject to cost-effectiveness, while smaller buildings remain at EPC E.
findings.matters: A change to the regulatory timetable that allows a council to defer and reallocate capital spending on commercial stock affects its forward capital programme and funding plans.
findings.figures: EPC C by April 2027 (removed); EPC B by 2031 for buildings over 1,000 sq m; EPC E current minimum
findings.quote: The 2027 Interim Milestone of EPC C was removed:

findings.paper_title: The Corporate Estate Annual Report FY25.26 FINAL
findings.headline: Corporate Estate office rental income rose 11.29% to £2,176,360 in FY25/26
findings.detail: The paper describes this as reversing previous stagnation in office income. It attributes the growth to rent reviews and an increase in the office portfolio, including the movement of Sovereign House into the estate.
findings.matters: Office income had been flat in previous years, and a reader comparing their own office estate with this one will want to know what drove the turnaround.
findings.quote: the office sector achieving an 11.29% increase to achieve £2,176,360 of revenue

findings.paper_title: The Corporate Estate Annual Report FY25.26 FINAL
findings.headline: Retail rents fell from £10.38 per sq ft in FY 24/25 to £9.12 per sq ft
findings.detail: The paper attributes the fall to market challenges, higher vacancy, and tenant failures. The Council's retail portfolio includes city centre retail and neighbourhood shops, and the paper says retail sector income declined slightly.
findings.matters: A fall in average retail rent of this size is a change in the income base that a finance director would want to see alongside the portfolio's overall rental growth.
findings.figures: £10.38 per sq ft (FY 24/25) to £9.12 per sq ft (FY25/26)
findings.quote: Retail rents have reduced slightly from £10.38 per sq ft in FY 24/25 to £9.12

findings.paper_title: The Corporate Estate Annual Report FY25.26 FINAL
findings.headline: Haymarket Shopping Centre gross income shows a slight reduction, excluding a £420,000 VAT adjustment made in FY2024/25
findings.detail: The paper says Net Operating Profit rose by £0.28m on FY24/25 and gross yield is above 25%. It also reports footfall year-to-date tracking down slightly on the same period in 2025.
findings.matters: The Haymarket is the estate's largest single retail asset, and a finance director would want to see whether its income is holding up once one-off adjustments are removed.
findings.figures: £420,000 VAT adjustment in FY2024/25; £0.28m increase in Net Operating Profit; over 25% gross yield; 1.2m footfall year-to-date
findings.quote: Excluding the VAT adjustment of £420,000 made in FY2024/25, gross income has shown a slight reduction in gross income.

daily_post.headline: The paper says Leicester's settlement produced a forecast change in Core Spending Power of 36.1% over 2024/25 to 2028/29, which is greater than the unitary authority average.
daily_post.lead: A finance director at another council can compare how the new funding formulas have changed their own core spending power.
